Mina had spent a month planning the astronomy club's first evening outdoors. She had chosen a field, borrowed a small telescope and made a list of things to observe. On the afternoon of the event, however, thick clouds spread across the sky. She wanted to cancel before anyone arrived.

Mr Green, the club adviser, asked what she had promised the visitors. “A chance to look at the night sky,” she said. “Not a guarantee that it would be clear,” he replied. He suggested explaining the situation and letting people decide whether to come. Mina sent a message describing the clouds and the indoor activities they could offer instead. Half the visitors still came.

At first, she kept apologising for the weather. Then a younger student asked how a telescope worked. Mina used two simple drawings to explain the parts. She had expected this explanation to take a minute, but the students' questions turned it into a lively discussion. Nobody was checking the clock to see how much time was left.

Later, a visitor noticed a small opening between the clouds. Mina quickly led the group outside. They took turns looking through the telescope before the gap closed. The view lasted only a few minutes, but the waiting had made everyone more attentive. Even the quietest student asked to look again.

While packing up, Mina found that her observation sheet was nearly empty. She had been too busy answering questions to record much. A visitor offered to share his notes, and several others added details. Together, they reconstructed a record of the night's brief view.

The evening had not followed Mina's plan, yet it had not been a failure. Her careful preparation had given her something to draw on when the weather changed. What helped most was involving the visitors in the new plan. She had arrived expecting to be the person with all the answers. She left with a record that belonged to the whole group and a better idea of what it meant to organise an event.

He suggested explaining the situation and letting people decide whether to come. Mina sent a message describing the clouds and the indoor activities they could offer instead. Later, a visitor noticed a small opening between the clouds. Mina quickly led the group outside. They took turns looking through the telescope before the gap closed. The view lasted only a few minutes, but the waiting had made everyone more attentive. Even the quietest student asked to look again.
